### Class weights and the meaning of mean

PyTorch 2.14 uses different denominators for class-index targets and
class-probability targets. Consider two examples with two classes,
class weights $w=(1,3)$, no label smoothing and no ignored targets:

| Quantity | A | B |
|---|---:|---:|
| Probabilities | $(0.8,0.2)$ | $(0.25,0.75)$ |
| Correct class | 0 | 1 |
| Class weight | 1 | 3 |
| $-\log p_y$ | $\approx0.223144$ | $\approx0.287682$ |

For class indices, the unreduced loss is
$\ell_n=-w_{y_n}\log p_{n,y_n}$. With `reduction="mean"`,
PyTorch divides its sum by the sum of target weights:

$$
\begin{aligned}
L_{\mathrm{index}}
&=\frac{\sum_n\ell_n}{\sum_n w_{y_n}}\\
&=\frac{-\log0.8-3\log0.75}{1+3}\\
&\approx0.271547.
\end{aligned}
$$

Now supply the same labels as probability vectors,
$q_A=(1,0)$ and $q_B=(0,1)$. The unreduced losses are unchanged.
For class probabilities, however, the mean divides by the number
of examples, $N=2$:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\ell_n&=-\sum_k w_kq_{nk}\log p_{nk},\\
L_{\mathrm{prob}}
&=\frac1N\sum_n\ell_n\\
&=\frac{-\log0.8-3\log0.75}{2}\\
&\approx0.543095.
\end{aligned}
$$

Changing the target representation has doubled the loss and its gradient
in this batch. Multiplying every class weight by ten leaves
$L_{\mathrm{index}}$ unchanged, because both numerator and denominator
scale by ten. It multiplies $L_{\mathrm{prob}}$ by ten.

The gradient of a weighted soft-target loss also needs the weights.
For one example, write $r_k=w_kq_k$ and $S=\sum_k r_k$. Then

$$
\begin{aligned}
\ell
&=S\log\sum_j e^{z_j}-\sum_k r_kz_k,\\
\frac{\partial\ell}{\partial z_j}
&=S\,p_j-r_j.
\end{aligned}
$$

A batch reduction subsequently divides this gradient by its denominator.
The earlier $p-q$ formula is the case of unit class weights and
normalized $q$.

The following NumPy calculation evaluates the two documented reductions;
it does not invoke the PyTorch API.

```python
class_weights = np.array([1., 3.])
weighted_logits = np.log([[.8, .2], [.25, .75]])
class_ids = np.array([0, 1])
probability_targets = np.eye(2)[class_ids]
weighted_log_p = log_softmax(weighted_logits)
nll = -weighted_log_p[np.arange(2), class_ids]
target_weights = class_weights[class_ids]
weighted_elements = -(probability_targets * class_weights * weighted_log_p).sum(axis=-1)

index_mean = np.sum(target_weights * nll) / target_weights.sum()
probability_mean = weighted_elements.mean()
assert np.allclose(weighted_elements, target_weights * nll)
assert np.isclose(index_mean, 0.27154744216738813)
assert np.isclose(probability_mean, 0.5430948843347763)
assert np.isclose(probability_mean, 2 * index_mean)

scaled_index_mean = np.sum(10 * target_weights * nll) / (10 * target_weights).sum()
scaled_probability_mean = (10 * weighted_elements).mean()
assert np.isclose(scaled_index_mean, index_mean)
assert np.isclose(scaled_probability_mean, 10 * probability_mean)
```

To use another weighting rule, request unreduced losses and explicitly
apply the desired mask, weights and denominator. When comparing runs,
record the target representation as well as class weights and reduction.

Source: [PyTorch 2.14, CrossEntropyLoss](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/2.14/generated/torch.nn.CrossEntropyLoss.html),
the separate equations for index and probability targets. The numerical
example and gradient calculation expand those equations.
